ex-105-1.title: Pressure exerted on a balloon
ex-105-1.question:
Two identical balloons are manipulated in two ways. One is squeezed by hand and the other is punctured with a pin. Assume the forces acting on each balloon are perpendicular to the balloon’s surface.

(a) If the area of balloon that is in contact with the hands is 1.6 × 10−2 m2, estimate the pressure exerted on the balloon by the hands when squeezing it with a total force of 80 N.

(b) If the pin exerts a force of 6 N on the balloon and the area of the pin’s tip is 4 × 10−6 m2, estimate the pressure exerted on the balloon by the pin.

ex-105-2.title: Air toy gun
ex-105-2.question: Initially, the body of an air toy gun contains 250 cm3 of air with an atmospheric pressure of 100 kPa. The soft bullet is installed on the outlet of the gun. When the body is pressed, the volume of the body decreases. The bullet will be expelled when the pressure of the air reaches 125 kPa. Find the volume of the air in the body when the bullet is expelled.
ex-105-2.answer:
By Boyle’s law,

p1V1 = p2V2

100 × 250 = 125 × V2

V2 = 200 cm3

The volume of the air in the body is 200 cm3.
ex-105-2.tips:
Tip

Express the same quantity in the same unit (p1 and p2 in kPa, and V1 and V2 in cm2 in this case).

ex-105-3.title: Investigating p−T relationship of a gas
ex-105-3.question:
Linda sets up the following apparatus to study the relationship between pressure p and temperature T of a fixed mass of gas at a constant volume (Fig a). The flask is heated by a water bath. The pressure of the air in the flask is measured by a Bourdon gauge at various temperatures. The result is plotted as a straight line graph as shown in Figure b.

(a) Estimate the absolute zero from the graph.

(b) Suggest what Linda should do to ensure the air in the flask reaches the same temperature as the water bath before the readings are taken.

(c) Linda believes that shortening the rubber tubing of the Bourdon gauge could improve the accuracy of the result. Is she correct? Explain briefly.

(d) Point out two more modifications that can improve the accuracy of the result.
ex-105-3.answer:
(a) Let θ °C be the absolute zero.

122 – 060 – θ = 137 – 122100 – 60

θ = −265

The absolute zero is −265 °C.

(b) She should stop heating the water bath and stir the water well. Then wait until the temperature is steady to take the readings.

(c) She is correct. Since the rubber tubing is not in direct contact with the water bath, the temperature of the air inside the tubing increases more slowly than that inside the flask and is probably lower than the readings taken. Shortening the rubber tubing can reduce the error due to this.

(d) The whole flask, including the neck, should be immersed in the water bath.

The thermometer should not touch the bottom of the beaker.

ex-105-4.title: Pressure inside an air-tight jar
ex-105-4.question: An air-tight jar contains a gas with a pressure of 100 kPa at 20 °C. If the jar is put in a refrigerator so that the temperature of the gas drops to 4 °C, what will be the gas pressure inside the jar?
ex-105-4.answer:
By pressure law,

p1T1 = p2T2

10020 + 273 = p24 + 273

p2 = 94.5 kPa

The gas pressure inside the jar is 94.5 kPa.
ex-105-4.tips:
Tip

Remember to convert °C to K and express p1 and p2 in the same unit (kPa in this case).

ex-105-5.title: Volume of air in a syringe
ex-105-5.question: A sealed syringe is filled with 30 cm3 of air at a temperature of 29 °C. The syringe is cooled to 4 °C in a freezer. What is the new volume of the air? Assume the air pressure inside the syringe remains constant.
ex-105-5.answer:
By Charles’ law,

V1T1 = V2T2

3029 + 273 = V24 + 273

V2 = 27.5 cm3

The new volume of the air is 27.5 cm3.
ex-105-5.tips:
Tip

Remember to convert the temperature from unit of °C to K.

ex-105-6.title: Using the general gas law to determine the change in pressure
ex-105-6.question:
Carbonated drinks are beverages that contain dissolved carbon dioxide. When a carbonated drink is shaken, the carbon dioxide molecules in the drink liquid escape into the space above the liquid and become carbon dioxide gas.

A sealed bottle of carbonated drink is shaken. Determine the change in gas pressure inside the bottle using the general gas law.
ex-105-6.answer:
When the dissolved carbon dioxide in the liquid drink changes to gas, the number of moles of gas in the bottle increases (n↑).

By pV = nRT, with the temperature and the volume of the gas in the bottle

remaining constant (T and V constant), the gas pressure inside the bottle

will increase (⇒ p↑).

ex-105-7.title: Hot air balloon
ex-105-7.question:
A hot air balloon has a fixed volume of 400 m3. Initially, the air is at a

temperature of 27 °C and a pressure of 100 kPa. Take R = 8.31 J mol−1 K−1

and NA = 6.02 × 1023 mol−1.

(a) Find

(i) the number of moles of gas molecules, and

(ii) the number of gas molecules

inside the balloon.

(b) The number of gas molecules inside the balloon changes when the gas is heated. If the gas is now heated to 120 °C and the balloon rises to an altitude so that the gas pressure becomes 80 kPa, what is the number of moles of gas molecules inside the balloon?
ex-105-7.answer:
(a) (i) By pV = nRT,

n = pVRT = (100 × 103)(400)(8.31)(27 + 273) = 16 040 mol ≈ 16 000 mol

There are 16 000 mol of gas molecules inside the balloon.

(ii) Number of gas molecules N

= nNA = 16 040 × (6.02 × 1023) = 9.66 × 1027

(b) By pV = nRT,

nTp = VR = constant

n1T1p1 = n2T2p2

(16 040)(27 + 273)100 = n2 × (120 + 273)80

n2 = 9800 mol

There are 9800 mol of gas molecules inside the balloon.
ex-105-7.tips:
Tip

Express p in Pa.

Tip

As this equation actually comes from the ratios of the quantities of the gas, you can express both p1 and p2 in kPa.

ex-105-8.title: Mixing gases
ex-105-8.question:
Two containers X and Y are connected by a short narrow tube with a closed tap as shown below. Both of them contain the same ideal gas. The number of moles of the gas in X is nX while that in Y is nY. The volume of X is three times that of Y while the pressure inside Y is three times that inside X. Assume the temperature of the gases is kept constant at T all the time.

(a) Find nXnY.

(b) The tap is opened to enable the gas to flow between the two containers.

(i) Describe the direction of the gas flow. Explain your answer.

(ii) After some time, the net flow of gas between the containers stops. Find the percentage change of the pressure inside X.
ex-105-8.answer:
(a) By pV = nRT, pVn = RT

Since the gases in X and Y have the same temperature,

pXVXnX = pYVYnY

nXnY = pXpY × VXVY = 13 × 31 = 1

(b) (i) Since Y is at a higher pressure, gas will flow from Y to X.

(ii) The net flow of gas stops when the pressures in X and Y become the same.

nX + nY = nX′ + nY′

pXVXRT + pYVYRT = p′VXRT + p′VYRT

pX(3VY) + (3pX)VY = p′(3VY) + p′VY

6pX = 4p’

p’ = 1.5pX

Percentage change = 1.5pX – pXpX × 100% = +50%
ex-105-8.tips:
Tip

The total number of gas molecules in X and Y should be unchanged.

Tip

RT is common to all terms on both sides and can be cancelled out.

ex-105-9.title: Root-mean-square speed
ex-105-9.question:
An ideal gas is sealed in a container of fixed volume. The gas is heated so that the root-mean-square speed crms of the gas molecules is doubled. The gas changes its temperature from T1 to T2 and its pressure from p1 to p2.

(a) Find p2 in terms of p1. It is given that crms = 3pVNm.

(b) Find T2 in terms of T1. It is given that crms = 3RTmNA.
ex-105-9.answer:
(a) By crms = 3pVNm, for constant V, N and m,

p2p1 = 2crmscrms = 2

p2 = 4p1

(b) By crms = 3RTmNA, for constant m,

T2T1 = 2crmscrms = 2

T2 = 4T1
ex-105-9.think: If the container is allowed to expand during the heating of the gas, will the answers to (a) and (b) change?
ex-105-9.thinkAnswer:
(a) Yes. For a fixed number of molecules, pV=13Nm crms2. Doubling the root-mean-square speed gives p2V2=4p1V1, so p2=4p1V1V2. If V2>V1, the final pressure is less than 4p1; its exact value requires the expansion volume.

(b) No. Since crms2∝ T, the absolute temperature still becomes T2=4T1, independent of the volume.

ex-105-10.title: Gas in a can
ex-105-10.question:
A sealed can of volume 350 cm3 contains an ideal gas at 115 kPa and 20 °C. Take the molar mass of the gas to be 29.0 g mol−1, and R to be 8.31 J mol−1 K−1.

(a) (i) Find the number of moles of gas in the can.

(ii) Find the root-mean-square speed of the gas molecules.

(iii) Find the kinetic energy of one mole of the gas molecules.

(b) The can is now placed in cold water and the gas inside is cooled to

5 °C. Find the change in the total kinetic energy of the gas molecules.
ex-105-10.answer:
(a) V = 350 cm3, p = 115 kPa, T = 20 °C, mNA = 29.0 g mol−1

(i) By pV = nRT,

n = pVRT = (115 × 103)(350 × 10–6)8.31 × (20 + 273) = 0.0165 mol

The number of moles of the gas is 0.0165 mol.

(ii) By 12mc2 = 3RT2NA,

c2¯ = 3RTmNA = 3 × 8.31 × (20 + 273)29.0 × 10–3 = 502 m s−1

The root-mean-square speed of the gas molecules is 502 m s−1.

(iii) KE of one mole of the gas

= NA × 3RT2NA = 32RT = 32 × 8.31 × (20 + 273) = 3650 J mol−1

(b) Total KE of the gas molecules

= N × 12mc2 = N × 3RT2NA = nNA × 3RT2NA = 32nRT

Change in total KE

= 32nR(T2 – T1) = 32 × 0.0165 × 8.31 × (5 – 20) = −3.09 J
ex-105-10.tips:
Tip

Write down the data provided in the question to determine the equation that should be applied.

Tip

Express mNA in kg mol−1.
